This automatic server selection mechanism is part of Spring Boot’s auto-configuration feature, which simplifies application setup and reduces manual configuration. Overall, Spring Boot intelligently manages embedded server selection by analyzing available dependencies and automatically configuring the most appropriate server for the application.

Que.q: Q57 : How can we disable the default server and enable the different one?
Que.a: In Spring Boot, we can disable the default embedded server and enable a different server by modifying the project dependencies in the Maven pom.xml or Gradle build file. By default, Spring Boot uses Apache Tomcat as the embedded server when we include the spring-boot-starter-web dependency. To switch to another server like Jetty or Undertow, we first exclude the default Tomcat dependency from the starter package. After excluding Tomcat, we add the dependency for the desired server, such as spring-boot-starter-jetty or spring-boot-starter-undertow. Once the new dependency is added, Spring Boot’s auto-configuration mechanism automatically detects and configures the new embedded server during application startup. This process does not require major code changes because Spring Boot handles the server configuration internally. Developers may choose different servers depending on performance requirements, scalability needs, memory usage, or application architecture. For example, Jetty is known for lightweight and scalable applications, while Undertow is often preferred for high-performance reactive applications. Switching servers in Spring Boot is simple because the framework separates application logic from server configuration. This flexibility allows developers to easily customize deployment environments according to project requirements while still benefiting from embedded server support and executable JAR packaging provided by Spring Boot.

Que.q: Q58 : What are the different Spring Boot annotations?
Que.a: Spring Boot provides many important annotations that simplify application development, configuration, dependency injection, REST API creation, scheduling, and asynchronous processing. Some of the most commonly used Spring Boot annotations are listed below :

list.@SpringBootApplication: This annotation combines @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan into a single annotation. It is mainly used on the main class to bootstrap and start a Spring Boot application.
list.@EnableAutoConfiguration: This annotation tells Spring Boot to automatically configure the application based on the dependencies available in the classpath.
list.@Configuration: The @Configuration annotation marks a class as a source of bean definitions for the Spring container.
list.@ComponentScan: This annotation tells Spring where to scan for components, services, repositories, and controllers automatically.
list.@Bean: The @Bean annotation is used inside a configuration class to explicitly define and manage beans in the Spring container.
list.@Component: The @Component annotation marks a class as a Spring-managed component so that it can be automatically detected and registered as a bean.
list.@Repository: The @Repository annotation marks a class as a data access layer component and provides exception translation for database operations.
list.@Service: The @Service annotation marks a class as a service layer component that contains business logic.
list.@Controller: The @Controller annotation is used to define web controllers that handle HTTP requests and return views.
list.@RestController: The @RestController annotation combines @Controller and @ResponseBody, allowing methods to directly return JSON or XML responses.
list.@RequestMapping: The @RequestMapping annotation maps HTTP requests to specific handler methods in controller classes.
list.@Autowired: The @Autowired annotation enables automatic dependency injection by allowing Spring to inject required beans automatically.
list.@PathVariable: The @PathVariable annotation extracts dynamic values from the URL path and maps them to method parameters.
list.@RequestParam: The @RequestParam annotation binds query parameters or form parameters from HTTP requests to method parameters.
list.@ResponseBody: The @ResponseBody annotation tells Spring to return the method result directly as the HTTP response body.
list.@RequestBody: The @RequestBody annotation converts the HTTP request body into a Java object.
list.@EnableWebMvc: The @EnableWebMvc annotation enables Spring MVC configuration and sets up components required for web applications.
list.@EnableAsync: The @EnableAsync annotation enables asynchronous method execution in Spring applications.
list.@Scheduled: The @Scheduled annotation is used to execute methods automatically at fixed intervals or based on cron expressions.
list.@EnableScheduling: The @EnableScheduling annotation enables scheduling support for methods annotated with @Scheduled.
